costGuide.title: Suzuki K14B Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a K14B typically takes 6-8 hours at £65-£75/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: The K14B is a simple, non-turbo petrol engine - replacement is relatively inexpensive. Coil pack and VVT solenoid condition are the main price drivers; a unit with documented recent replacements will command a premium. The engine is widely available from Suzuki breakers, and parts commonality with the K12M and K15B ensures good supply. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide for detailed breakdowns.

failures.title: Suzuki K14B Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Coil Pack Failure - 40,000-80,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The K14B's ignition coil packs are a known weak point. They fail due to heat cycling and age, causing misfires, rough running, and the engine management light illuminating. Symptoms include hesitation under acceleration and reduced fuel economy. This is the most common K14B issue.
items.repairVsReplace: Coil pack replacement is straightforward and costs £100-£250 for a set (four coils). Replacing all four at once is recommended, as they tend to fail sequentially. Read our full ignition system failure guide.

items.title: VVT Solenoid / Oil Control Valve Issues - 60,000-100,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The K14B's variable valve timing (VVT) system uses an oil control valve (OCV) that can become clogged with sludge or suffer from electrical failure. Symptoms include poor low-end response, rough idle, and engine management light with VVT-related error codes. This is often caused by infrequent oil changes or incorrect oil viscosity.
items.repairVsReplace: The VVT solenoid can be cleaned or replaced - cost typically £100-£300. A full timing chain inspection is recommended if the VVT system has been compromised by oil contamination.

items.title: Timing Chain Wear - 80,000-120,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The K14B uses a maintenance-free timing chain. While generally reliable, chain wear can occur in engines with poor oil maintenance or high mileage. Symptoms include a rattling noise on cold start, which disappears as oil pressure builds. If ignored, the chain can skip or snap - catastrophic for the engine.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, chain and tensioner replacement costs £600-£1,200. If the chain has skipped or snapped, full engine replacement is the only option.

items.title: Thermostat Housing Cracking - 60,000-100,000 miles
items.whatHappens: The K14B's plastic thermostat housing can develop cracks over time, leading to coolant leaks. Symptoms include low coolant levels, engine overheating, and visible coolant drips near the thermostat housing.
items.repairVsReplace: Thermostat housing replacement costs £150-£300. It's a relatively straightforward repair, but coolant system flushing should be performed at the same time.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2010 K14B units received revised coil pack design and updated VVT calibration. Timing chain wear appears less common on later units with regular oil changes.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Suzuki K14B
variants.intro: The K14B is part of Suzuki's K-series engine family, sharing its basic architecture with the K12M (1.2L), K14C (1.4L turbo), and K15B (1.5L). It was produced in two main output variants - 92 hp (European market) and 95 hp (some export markets) - but the block and internals are identical. Where to find your engine code: The engine code is stamped on a metal plate on the cylinder block, visible from the top of the engine bay. The engine number on the V5C starts with K14B followed by seven digits. Alternatively, check the vehicle identification plate or use the registration lookup above. Commonly confused codes: - K14C - The 1.4-litre Boosterjet turbo that replaced the K14B. It's a completely different engine family - turbocharged, direct-injection, with different mounting points and electrical architecture. Not a direct swap. - K12M - The 1.2-litre Dualjet, found in Swift, Baleno, and other Suzuki models. It has the same basic architecture but smaller displacement - physically similar but different block and ECU. - K15B - The 1.5-litre Dualjet, found in later Vitara and S-Cross models. Similar block architecture but larger displacement and different ECU calibration. Why getting the right code matters: The K14B is a simple, naturally aspirated engine - it's not directly swappable with the K14C Boosterjet (turbo, different cooling and exhaust routing) or the K12M (different displacement). Always match the engine code exactly when buying a replacement.

relatives.description: : The K12M was the 1.2-litre DualJet predecessor, fitted to earlier Swift and Baleno models. It shares the same K-series architecture but with smaller displacement and lower power output (90 hp vs 95 hp). The K12M is simpler, lacking some of the K14B's VVT refinement, but is generally more fuel-efficient.

: The K14C Boosterjet turbo completely replaced the naturally aspirated K14B from 2015. It's a fundamentally different engine - turbocharged, direct-injection, with 140 hp and significantly more torque. The K14C resolved many of the K14B's VVT and coil pack issues but introduced its own set of turbo-related complexities. If you're considering swapping a K14B for a K14C, the engine mounts, exhaust, cooling system, and ECU are all different - not a straightforward replacement.

relatives.code: None: The K14B is a Suzuki

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Suzuki K14B - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used K14B makes sense for lower-value Swift and SX4 examples (pre-2010, high-mileage, sub-£2,000 values). Used units from £300-£700 are widely available from Suzuki breakers. However, a used K14B only makes sense with documented service history and coil pack replacement - an unknown-history unit will likely need immediate coil pack replacement (£100-£250) and VVT solenoid inspection (£100-£300). Link: used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper K14B recon (£800-£1,500) addresses the specific weaknesses of this engine - new coil packs, fully cleaned VVT system, new timing chain and tensioner, and rebuilt cylinder head. For most Swift and SX4 owners, this is the sweet spot - reliable, warrantied, and well within the vehicle's value on most examples. Link: reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full K14B rebuild (£1,500-£2,500) is justified for low-mileage, well-maintained examples or where the owner wants to preserve a well-loved car. An upgraded rebuild should include new coil packs, a new thermostat housing, a new timing chain kit, and a fully overhauled cylinder head. Link: rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All our vetted UK Suzuki specialists offer supply-only or full supply-and-fit on K14B units - fitted prices include 6-8 hours of labour, specialist fluids, and a 12-24 month warranty. Nationwide delivery covers supply-only orders. Link: supply and fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The K14B sits in host vehicles with UK market values ranging from £800 (early Swift 1.4 with high mileage) to £5,000 (late SX4 with low mileage) . If your K14B host is worth less than £1,500, a reconditioned K14B at £800-£1,500 will represent 50-100% of the vehicle's value. In this bracket, a used unit with documented coil pack history at £300-£700 is often the more financially rational choice. For hosts above £3,000, the reconditioned unit is the clear winner - adding several years of life to a car worth keeping.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the Suzuki K14B engine?
items.answer: Coil pack failure is the most common K14B problem, occurring from 40,000-80,000 miles . It causes misfires, rough running, and the engine management light illuminating. VVT solenoid issues are the second most common - they cause poor low-end response and rough idle. Both are relatively inexpensive to fix. Coil pack replacement costs £100-£250 for a set; VVT solenoid cleaning or replacement costs £100-£300; replacing all four coil packs at once is recommended.

items.question: Which Suzuki models use the K14B engine?
items.answer: The K14B powers multiple Suzuki models from 2005-2015: Swift (I and II generations), SX4, Grand Vitara, Splash, Ignis, and Wagon R+. All wear the 1.4 VVT badge. Swift and SX4 were the highest‑volume UK applications. The engine was discontinued in 2015 when the K14C Boosterjet replaced it. Always confirm the engine code on the V5C before buying a replacement.

items.question: Can I fit a K14C Boosterjet engine in place of my K14B?
items.answer: Not easily. While both are 1.4-litre K-series engines, the K14C is turbocharged, direct-injection, and has different engine mounts, exhaust routing, cooling system, and ECU architecture. Fitting a K14C would require replacing the engine loom, ECU, engine mounts, exhaust manifold, and potentially the gearbox. The cost is prohibitive - it's cheaper to buy a factory‑spec K14B or sell the car and buy a K14C-equipped model. Engine mounts are different; ECU calibration is completely different; turbocharger requires different oil and cooling lines; not recommended - buy the correct K14B.

items.question: How many miles can a Suzuki K14B engine last?
items.answer: With regular oil changes and timely coil pack replacement, a K14B can exceed 150,000-200,000 miles. The timing chain is the main variable - some last 200,000 miles, others need replacement at 80,000. The key is strict 10,000‑mile oil changes using the correct 5W‑30 oil and replacing coil packs at the first sign of misfire. Coil pack replacement at 60,000 miles extends lifespan; timing chain inspection recommended at 80,000 miles; VVT solenoid cleaning at 60,000 miles prevents issues.
